findings.reason: I checked fitQuasiIndependenceModel. Line 87 skips zero cells, so support is only the observed cells, and lines 171/182 rescale factors to match row and column totals. A reviewer with one support cell therefore gets E = rowTotal = M, so the residual at line 329 is 0 and the check at line 330 fails. The old test with bob→alice ×10 was rewritten into a 2x2 cycle fixture to keep a flag, which shows exclusive pairs no longer flag.
findings.claim: The quasi-independence fit uses only positive cells, so a pair where the reviewer reviews only one author, or the author has only one reviewer, is fitted exactly (E = M, residual 0) and can never be flagged.
findings.evidence: fitQuasiIndependenceModel builds its support only from cells with count > 0 (`if (count === 0) continue;`) and rescales each reviewer factor with `reviewerFactors[reviewerPosition] *= rowTotal / fittedRowTotal` (line 171). For a reviewer with a single support cell, that forces E_ij = rowTotal = M_ij, and the column step does the same for an author with a single reviewer. Trigger: 50 PRs by alice, each reviewed only by bob, plus any other unrelated pairs. Then E(bob,alice) = 50, `pearsonResidual = (count - fittedCount)/Math.sqrt(fittedCount)` = 0, and `count > fittedCount && pearsonResidual > threshold` is false at every allowed threshold (≥0.5). The removed z-score code would have flagged bob→alice. More generally, flagging is possible only when the support graph has a cycle. No locked test covers an exclusive pair, and docs/statistics.md and the HTML explanation don't disclose this blind spot.

members.claim: The quasi-independence model is fit only on cells that have a positive observed count, and it is forced to match each row and column total. Any reviewer who reviewed only one author, or any author reviewed by only one reviewer, therefore gets E_ij = M_ij exactly, so the residual is 0. The same happens for every cell when a connected component's support is a tree (cells = rows + cols - 1). As a result the clearest bias pattern — reviewer X reviews only author Y, e.g. 20 times — can never be flagged, though the old z-score would have flagged it. Real review graphs are sparse, so a large share of cells are fit exactly and the detector loses most of its power. This regression isn't mentioned in the PR or the docs, and no test covers it.

findings.reason: Lines 329-330 apply only `count > fittedCount && residual > threshold`, with no floor on count or E. Example with full 2x2 support: A→X 1000, A→Y 1, B→X 1, B→Y 1 gives E(B,Y) ≈ 2·2/1003 ≈ 0.004, so a single review has a residual of about 15 and is flagged.
findings.claim: There is no minimum count or minimum expected count, so a one-review pair with a tiny fitted E can produce a large Pearson residual and be flagged.
findings.evidence: The Pearson residual (M-E)/sqrt(E) is compared with the threshold without any minimum on count or expected count. In large, sparse interaction graphs the fitted E for a cell can be well below 1. A pair with only one review and E < ~0.17 then has a residual above the default threshold of 2.0 and is reported as 'bias'. The Pearson approximation isn't valid for such small expected counts, so this produces noisy false positives on one-off pairs. Consider requiring a minimum count or minimum expected count.

findings.reason: Lines 322-357 wrap both the fit call and the flagging loop, and the catch is unconditional. A TypeError in the loop would become a modelFitError instead of failing loudly. This is a maintainability concern, so it stays low.
findings.claim: The try/catch wraps the flagging loop as well as the fit and catches every exception, which can hide programming errors as 'model could not be fit'.
findings.evidence: The try/catch wraps the flagging loop as well as the IPF fit, and it catches every exception. Any programming error, such as a TypeError, is silently turned into a 'model could not be fit' result instead of failing loudly. For finite positive counts the fit can't actually fail, so this path mostly hides bugs. Limit the catch to the fit call, or to known convergence/validation errors.
